chunks: Al-Asbagh ibn Nubatah narrated from the Commander of the Faithful (peace be upon him):
That he ruled: 'A restriction (on financial transactions) is placed on the boy until he matures/reaches understanding.'
And he (peace be upon him) ruled regarding debt: 'The debtor is imprisoned; if his insolvency and need become clear, his path is cleared (released) until he acquires wealth.'

And he (peace be upon him) ruled regarding a man who evades his creditors: 'He is imprisoned, then an order is issued regarding him, and his wealth is divided among his creditors in shares; if he refuses, he is sold and the proceeds are divided among them.'

key_terms.إِفْلاَسُهُ: Insolvency or bankruptcy of the debtor
key_terms.اَلْحَجْر: Legal restriction or guardianship preventing a person from managing their own finances
key_terms.اَلْغُلاَم: The boy or minor, specifically in the context of financial maturity
key_terms.يَلْتَوِي: He evades or twists himself away (from paying debts)

ai.seo_question: What are the Islamic legal rulings regarding debt imprisonment and insolvency?
ai.summary: Recorded in Al-Tusi’s *Tahdhib al-Ahkam*, this hadith details Imam Ali’s (AS) pragmatic judicial approach to financial disputes, emphasizing the distinction between temporary inability and permanent insolvency (*iflas*). It establishes a legal framework where imprisonment serves as a pressure mechanism rather than a punitive end, ensuring creditors are compensated while protecting the debtor’s dignity and future earning capacity. This ruling reflects the Shia jurisprudential principle of balancing justice with mercy, preventing perpetual debt bondage.
